Figure 5:Attention ablation and selected TunnelingNet configurations.Rows show (a) narrow generation, (b) estimation/reconstruction,
(c) conditional control, and (d) inverse rendering. Curves plot validation
MSE (lower is better) against optimizer updates; thin/thick traces denote
measurements/nine-point moving averages, and (b–d) use logarithmic
horizontal axes. Under matched parameters, data, optimizer, batch size, and
schedule, NJA is preferred for the RGB target. For the three structured
non-RGB targets, MTA produces clean, recognizable outputs in 27–47 minutes
with19.019.0–38.5×38.5\timesfewer updates, while NJA remains pale or fragmented
after 777–930 minutes; recognizable structure appears7777–100×100\timesearlier. These endpoint time gaps of16.616.6–34.1×34.1\timesare conservative
because NJA has not reached comparable quality. The legacy NJA previews in
(c,d) use different evaluation examples; all Edge maps use the same
grayscale reader. The rightmost cards summarize the deployed mapping,
attention topology, and RGB-evidence route.

Figure 6:Native-reference routing can override current geometry.True 10-step inference from the TunnelingNet 270 native-reference run. At update
500, conflicting poses produce duplicate limbs; at update 2,200, the output
still retains the RGB1pose instead of following the current Normal.

Figure 7:Qualitative effects of task-dependent structural choices.Each row uses an evaluation example from one of the four interfaces.
(a,c) compare NJA with MTA for estimation/reconstruction and conditional
control. (b) compares native-reference and first-RGB-condition routing
under NJA for narrow generation. (d) compares condition-side and
target-only tunnel placement for inverse rendering. Green borders mark the visually preferred outputs in the displayed
comparisons. The highlighted outputs in rows (b) and (d) use 200 and 100
optimizer updates, reached in 45 min 32 s and 27 min 18 s, respectively.
In (b), the condition-branch result follows the Normal/Pose condition while
retaining the appearance supplied by RGB1; the deployed TunnelingNet follows the
slightly lower validation MSE and uses the native reference route reported
in Table2. Checkpoint indices are shown
above outputs.

Figure 8:Qualitative effects of rectified-flow objective shaping.At update 250, each row compares plain rectified flow, single-step
clean-latent prediction, high-noise anchoring, multi-resolution noise, and
the ground truth. With batch size one and no gradient accumulation, each
model has completed only 250 optimizer steps and trained on exactly250 sampled examples. High-noise anchoring is the only shared choice that
preserves both Normal saturation and sparse Edge structure. Green borders
mark the selected objective; all Edge maps use the same grayscale reader.

Figure 9:Rapid acquisition across the first 200 updates.Rows correspond to estimation, narrow generation, conditional control, and
inverse rendering. Columns show true 10-step Euler inference from pure noise
after 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, and 200 updates. Times below the column headings
report the observed wall-clock range across the four tasks, including
scheduled diagnostics. Each row reuses one fixed evaluation example and the
same inference seed. With batch size one and no gradient accumulation,each update uses exactly one sampled training example; thus even the
final column has seen only 200 examples. No condition or ground-truth image
is displayed. Edge outputs use the same per-image contrast stretch for
visibility.

Figure 11:Paired cross-modal matrix, Part II: physical and material
properties (273 pairs; 546 TunnelingNets).Each cell places conditional control in
the upper-left triangle and RGB-assisted inverse rendering in the
lower-right. Continuous entries useQS=1−decoded MSE\mathrm{QS}=1-\text{decoded MSE}; categorical entries display
DAcc. Triangle colors encode QS for continuous outputs and DAcc for
categorical outputs on a
common zero-to-one scale. Cells markedN/A are unavailable
in the current release.

Figure 12:Paired cross-modal matrix, Part III: visual structure,
motion, and pose (100 pairs; 200 TunnelingNets).Diagonal cell ordering and metrics
follow Figure11. Separating this family from
the global matrix enlarges pose, geometry, and semantic annotations while
preserving their original input–output coordinates. Cells markedN/A are unavailable in the current release.

Figure 16:Qualitative comparison for InterfacesAandBon the post-release evaluation set.Each row contains a different crop-aligned example evaluated in
Table9. Panel (a) compares every
relative-depth method, with depth maps displayed after the affine alignment
used by the evaluation protocol. Panel (b) compares every conditional RGB
method under identical edge conditions, RGB references, and targets. WSM is
the rightmost column, outlined in blue.

Figure 17:Qualitative comparison for InterfaceCon the
post-release evaluation set.The three task blocks correspond to Normal→\rightarrowEdge, Relative
Depth→\rightarrowNormal, and Edge→\rightarrowHuman Segmentation in
Table9. Within each four-column group,
the input and target are followed by the MODUS and WSM predictions. WSM
outputs are outlined in blue. The same spatial crop is applied to all four
images within each group. For human segmentation, the target and both
predictions are shown as binary human-foreground masks.

Figure 18:Qualitative comparison for InterfacesAandBunder independent public annotation conventions.The rows use the same scene crops and order as
Figure16. Panel (a) replaces
the relative-depth target with Depth Anything V2; predictions use the same
fixed method-level near–far convention and percentile normalization as
the quantitative evaluation.
Panel (b) is unchanged because the post-release experiment already used
OpenCV Canny as the Edge condition. WSM is the rightmost column, outlined
in blue.

Figure 19:Qualitative comparison for InterfaceCunder
independent public annotation conventions.The three task blocks correspond to Relative Depth→\rightarrowNormal,
Normal→\rightarrowHuman Segmentation, and Normal→\rightarrowEdge in
Table10. Each four-column
group shows the independently annotated input and target followed by the
MODUS and WSM predictions generated from that input. WSM outputs are
outlined in blue.

Figure 20:Qualitative Part I: anatomy of the four WSM interfaces.The four rows correspond to RGB-to-WSG estimation/reconstruction,
WSG-to-WSG conditional control, text+WSG narrow generation, and RGB-assisted
inverse rendering. Each row retains the actual condition, prediction, and
ground truth in a common three-column layout. For interfaces that consume
auxiliary RGB evidence, the RGB context appears as a labeled inset inside
the primary condition. All outputs are true 10-step samples initialized
from Gaussian noise.

Figure 21:Qualitative Part II: RGB estimation of geometry and motion.Six TunnelingNets recover relative and absolute depth, normals, curvature, edges,
and optical flow. Curvature is shown explicitly rather than being absorbed
into a generic geometry example; the row-local keys make scalar, vector,
and boundary encodings directly interpretable.

Figure 22:Qualitative Part III: RGB estimation of articulated pose structure.DWPose, SMPL-X, MediaPipe Pose, XPose, MediaPipe Seg, and Universal
Pose expose complementary skeleton, surface, region, and category-independent
articulation representations. The examples retain sparse limb topology and
body extent rather than judging articulated structure only through dense
pixel similarity.For MediaPipe Pose (3D pose), we
deliberately retain an example with incomplete pseudo ground truth: the
generated result uses its learned prior to recover missing structure and
can therefore surpass the automatic annotation.

Figure 23:Qualitative Part IV: RGB estimation of physical object properties.Seven object-aligned fields cover solid and surface volume, weight, support,
static friction force, density, and friction coefficient. These outputs
test whether spatial support remains stable while the predicted physical
quantity changes.

Figure 24:Qualitative Part V: RGB estimation of material and PBR appearance (1/2).Ambient and diffuse color, opacity, specular color, shininess, base color,
and diffuse response separate spatial material support from the value
assigned within it.

Figure 25:Qualitative Part V: RGB estimation of material and PBR appearance (2/2).Height, roughness, metallicity, specular response, and opacity maps
complete the PBR interface. Prediction and ground truth use the same
channel-specific encoding in every row.

Figure 26:Qualitative Part VI: RGB estimation of segmentation and semantics.Alpha support, object category, container, and multi-class semantic masks
isolate the spatial and categorical aspects
of segmentation. The categorical rows show selected successful cases;
aggregate accuracy remains reported by the quantitative matrices.

Figure 27:Qualitative Part VII: geometry-conditioned narrow RGB generation (1/2).Relative depth, absolute depth, normals, curvature, and edges supply the
target-frame structure. Historical RGB context is embedded inside the
condition panel and never substitutes for the evaluation target frame.

Figure 28:Qualitative Part VII: motion- and pose-conditioned narrow RGB generation (2/2).DWPose, SMPL-X, MediaPipe pose and MediaPipe Seg, and XPose test whether sparse,
articulated, or semantic pose conditions redirect the generated frame while
text and the historical reference preserve scene identity.

Figure 29:Qualitative Part VIII: physics-, semantic-, and material-conditioned narrow RGB generation (1/4).Object class, volume, weight, support, and friction fields begin the
exhaustive non-geometric source sweep.

Figure 30:Qualitative Part VIII: physics-, semantic-, and material-conditioned narrow RGB generation (2/4).Material class, density, friction coefficient, container, entity category,
ambient color, and diffuse color test controls whose information is
concentrated inside object support rather than distributed across the image.

Figure 31:Qualitative Part VIII: physics-, semantic-, and material-conditioned narrow RGB generation (3/4).Base color, diffuse response, height, roughness, and metallicity show how
appearance controls interact with text and RGB context.

Figure 32:Qualitative Part VIII: physics-, semantic-, and material-conditioned narrow RGB generation (4/4).Specular response, opacity maps, and semantic masks complete the 33
visually readable narrow-generation source modalities.

Figure 33:Qualitative Part IX: representative WSG conditional control (1/6).Six geometry-to-geometry transfers cover depth, normals, curvature, edges,
and flow without auxiliary RGB evidence.

Figure 34:Qualitative Part IX: representative WSG conditional control (2/6).Geometry-to-pose and pose-to-geometry mappings test whether dense surface
structure and sparse articulated structure can supervise one another.

Figure 35:Qualitative Part IX: representative WSG conditional control (3/6).All six directed conversions among DWPose, SMPL-X, and MediaPipe pose are
shown, exposing the common articulated structure beneath distinct encodings.

Figure 36:Qualitative Part IX: representative WSG conditional control (4/6).Four physical-property transfers probe volume, weight, support, density,
and friction while preserving object-aligned spatial support.

Figure 37:Qualitative Part IX: representative WSG conditional control (5/6).Four material-to-physics and physics-to-material mappings test whether
shared object support is sufficient for translation between distinct value
spaces; two categorical rows test label-aware transport.

Figure 38:Qualitative Part IX: representative WSG conditional control (6/6).Four PBR conversions isolate translation among base color, diffuse,
roughness, metallicity, and specular response.

Figure 39:Qualitative Part X: representative RGB-assisted inverse rendering (1/6).Geometry-to-geometry transfers repeat Part IX with observed RGB evidence,
making scene-specific boundaries and identity available to the TunnelingNet.

Figure 40:Qualitative Part X: representative RGB-assisted inverse rendering (2/6).Geometry-to-pose and pose-to-geometry mappings show how RGB evidence resolves
structure that is underdetermined by the first condition alone.

Figure 41:Qualitative Part X: representative RGB-assisted inverse rendering (3/6).Six directed pose conversions retain their explicit condition while using
the RGB observation to recover scene-specific body extent and visibility.

Figure 42:Qualitative Part X: representative RGB-assisted inverse rendering (4/6).Physical-property mappings combine object-aligned structured evidence with
RGB boundaries to stabilize support and predicted value.

Figure 43:Qualitative Part X: representative RGB-assisted inverse rendering (5/6).Four cross-family transfers show where visible object identity complements
the structured input; two categorical rows retain label-aware evaluation.

Figure 44:Qualitative Part X: representative RGB-assisted inverse rendering (6/6).Four PBR conversions complete the 32-mapping RGB-assisted slice of the
family of 536 TunnelingNets.

Figure 45:Qualitative Part XI: categorical outputs.One verified example is retained for each of the five
categorical targets. Each row shows the condition, the final output of the
complete categorical TunnelingNet, and the corresponding ground truth.
